text_fidelity_a:
Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black I really like this GPS sports watch so far. Garmin makes a huge range of sports watches. This vivoactive HR is one of their lower priced GPS watches. It doesn't have the more advanced sports training features or build quality of the more expensive Garmin Fenix and Forerunner watches. However, for this price, you do get GPS and smartwatch features in addition to basic fitness tracking.

I tried the GPS mode on a 3-hour bike ride, running my dedicated bicycle computer at the same time. Distance calculations of the 2 units were less than 1 mile different, which I think is very good for small portable units like this. Current speed was always about the same, though looking at the watch to see your speed while riding is kind of difficult, especially compared to the big display on my handlebar-mounted bike computer. You can mount the watch on your bicycle handlebar, but that would of course disable the heart rate tracking feature of the watch. The wrist-based heart rate monitor is not as accurate as a chest-strap heart rate monitor, with a slower response time that is very apparent during interval training (short bursts of high-intensity effort), but you can connect an ANT+ HR monitor to this watch to improve accuracy.

GPS mode has an advertised battery life of 16 hours, which I think is really terrific for a gadget of this size. My 3 hour bike ride burned about 20% of the battery on the vivo, so 16 hours of GPS time is plausible. Garmin also advertises 8 days of battery life with the GPS turned off, but realistically, who buys a $250 GPS watch and never turns on the GPS? Still, I expect to get in at least a couple of long bike rides or several runs before having to recharge this watch. Recharging is very quick using the USB charging cradle included with the watch. Because battery life is so good, you don't need a spare charger for your office like you might need with the Apple smartwatch.

If you have a (free) Garmin account, you can upload your daily activity to the Garmin server so you can review it on their website afterwards. This is useful for tracking your fitness progress (speed, distance, etc) over time.

The smartwatch features are pretty basic (compared to dedicated smartwatches from Apple or Google), showing phone call caller-ID and copying notifications from your smartphone (via Bluetooth) and displaying them on the watch. If you like checking your notifications quickly and don't want to pull your phone out every time it beeps, getting them on your watch is great. If I'm jogging or in a business meeting or at dinner but am expecting an important message, I can just glance at the watch and quickly ignore it if it isn't important. I have my notifications for high-priority emails, SMS, and a couple of messaging apps synced with my phone. This seems to work mostly flawlessly with my Samsung smartphone. Occasionally, the notifications will stop working but restarting my phone fixes that. I don't know if that is a problem with the phone's base software or with the Garmin app that runs on my phone. The Garmin app that runs on your smartphone lets you pick which app's notifications to show on the watch. I do not know how this works with Apple phones. There are some other smartwatch apps like weather forecasts and calendar, but I'm not sure if scrolling through these on your small watch face is really easier than pulling out your phone to view the app on the larger screen there.

If you're comparing this Garmin watch to an Apple smartwatch, yes Apple has a lot more apps, but Garmin has an 8 day battery life compared to less than 1 day for Apple. Personally, battery life is more valuable to me since there are not yet any killer apps for the Apple watch. Having a dead watch because you forgot to charge it the night before is not fun. Also, the Garmin watch has a built-in GPS, while the Apple watch does not. This means you can record a bike ride or run carrying only the watch, not your phone as well.

Garmin also has basic fitness tracking features like resting heart rate, sleep tracking, intensive exercise tracking, step counting, etc. If you're active enough to want to spend money a GPS sports watch (instead of a cheap fitness band), I don't think the step counting is going to be interesting to you. I bike or run at least 10 hours every week of the year and steps have no interest to me. Resting heart rate is an indicator of your health and fitness and I'm looking forward to tracking that. Intensive exercise tracking may also be useful if you tend to slack off during your exercise. Sleep tracking is reportedly not too accurate on this watch (it can't tell if you're really sleeping or reading a book in bed), but that isn't something that greatly interests me.

On the subjective side, this chunky plastic rectangular watch does look like a fitness tracker rather than a real watch. The much better looking Garmin Fenix looks like something you could wear to the office, but this watch maybe not. At least the vivoactive has a very comfortable wristband that should fit well on a range of wrist sizes.

Again, this is one of Garmin's cheaper GPS watches. I think the features and performance are great for this price point, but if you're involved in hard core training program, you should definitely look at the features of some of Garmin's better GPS watches.

I would have given this watch 5 stars for functionality and value for the price if it was better looking, but Garmin seems to have made it intentionally ugly in try to upsell you on their better looking and more expensive Fenix and Forerunner watches.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black

I love being able to link our Fire Sticks to Alexa. We have a Dot in the guest room and the original Echo in the master bedroom controlling both Fire Sticks. This one also works on verbal commands through the remote, but you have to think about what you ask for if you have several streaming services. We have Prime, Netflix, Hulu, HBO Go and DirectTV Now (still saving $165 a month over cable!) and Alexa can find a specific show, but perhaps not on the channel you wanted.

Comparing the Fire Stick and the Roku Express is pretty simple. The layout for the two is completely different and I actually think the Roku is easier to sort through and find stuff. It feels less cluttered actually. I do appreciate the full integration of the Fire Stick with my other devices through our Amazon account - I can pick up a show on Prime with my tablet, phone or tv exactly where I left off. Regardless of which streaming stick we use, we're still incredibly happy we dumped the cable.

I use them in my Endless Pool, so I don't know how they will perform in regular pool during turns and flips, but my guess is because of their lightness they will work fine. text_fidelity_a:
Elgood Tabletop Vacuum Cleaner with Cleaning Brush,Eraser dust Vacuum USB Charging,Best Desk Vacuum No Dead Angle Cleaning(Green) Like many single guys I have various pockets of dust scattered around my place. My desk, behind the computer towers and monitors where all the cords are piled up is one of the worst. So a handheld vacuum to clean all those nooks and crannies sounded like a good idea. Sadly, this is not the portable vacuum that I am looking for.

A few design flaws were obvious as soon as I took this out of the box and started charging it. There is no stand or holder for the vacuum so it has to sit directly on the brushes you've just been cleaning with. The light indicating when the vacuum is charging/fully charged is pinhole size, barely visible from any distance. So I had to go pick it up and squint at the light to see if it was charged up. The little brush for cleaning the inside of the vacuum is one more tiny thing to keep track of and is easily lost.

Even more flaws became obvious as soon as I tried to use the vacuum. With the nozzle on I tried to clean the back of my desk where all the computer wires are. The nozzle immediately jammed up on hair and dust balls. That area is still as dusty now as it was before I tried to vacuum it. Next I tried cleaning some flat surfaces. The brushes pushed the dust back and forth while barely vacuuming any of it up. I put my hand across the bottom of the brushes and could not feel any suction at all. When I put my finger right into the center hole that the dust was supposed to be scooped up into, I could barely feel a tiny amount of suction. I still very much like the idea of a handheld vacuum but I very much do not like this one and cannot recommend it to anyone.
text_fidelity_b: Elgood Tabletop Vacuum Cleaner with Cleaning Brush,Eraser dust Vacuum USB Charging,Best Desk Vacuum No Dead Angle Cleaning(Green)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech MK550 Wireless Wave Keyboard and Mouse Combo - Includes Keyboard and Mouse, Long Battery Life, Ergonomic Wave Design, Black This is my first wireless keyboard and I love it. The black keyboard feature is designed with the wave feature meant to guide the hands and fingers into place. This, however is not something I notice. The wave is very minimal as not to confuse the hands from your last keyboard. I like the padded wrist rest. The wrist, ergonomically, is supposed to be level with the keys. The keyboard is comfortable! The contour grip on the side of the mouse feels good and secure.

What is good is that the battery claims to have a life-span of 3-year keyboard and 2 year mouse. That is a long time so as not to be bothered. What I enjoy on the keyboard are the touch controls. Press the key with the camera and your Windows Photo files come up. You can control the ITUNES with a press of several buttons on the keyboard, louder, previous and next songs, etc. I also am impressed with the push of the calculator button and up pops the Windows calculator without having to search for it in the Windows programs.

I was leary of this wave-thing, hoping it wasn't like the old heavily structured ergo keyboards, and to my surprise it was a breeze to use. I love it, works great! ....Rizzo

In order to use both the mouse and the keyboard, you insert a single, small dongle into a USB port on a laptop or PC. Both the mouse and the keyboard connect to that same dongle to allow you to use them wirelessly.

Both the mouse and the keyboard work really well. I have not had any problems with either one of them.

The one negative is the expense and hassle of putting a battery in both of them.

My desk looks neater, the dock gives me all the ports I need on a daily basis without having to use multiple adapters, and it charges my laptop.

LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).

text_fidelity_a:
Magellan Triton 400 Waterproof Hiking GPS UPDATE 11-30-2009: I initially gave this unit a rating of 3 stars. I am upgrading it to 4 stars because of a firmware upgrade that vastly improved the speed of the unit and eliminated issues I saw with VantagePoint. That said, I am leaving my original write-up intact.

---

I am an avid geocacher, and I have other hand-held units by Garmin and DeLorme. I have never used a Magellan GPS though I have friends who have used an Explorist for years with reasonable results. I was anxious to try out this unit to see if Magellan puts out a good product. In a nutshell, it is a mixed bag though overall the Triton 400 is a nice unit.

This is a very small unit, a little smaller than my Garmin eTrex Legend which is a fairly simple unit. Small is not necessarily a bad thing. It fits nicely in a pocket or a stash bag, being about the size of a cell phone.

The display is small too and people who want a large display will not like this unit. That said, the display is very bright, crisp and clear, everything being quite visible and readable. It had, in my opinion, the best general display of the units I have used, surpassing even the DeLorme in display quality.

Once the unit is powered on, it quickly starts finding satellites. Though it switches to navigation mode quickly, it is important to remember that the unit may or may not have a good lock on satellites - it may still be acquiring more. Be cautious in this regard, until used to using this unit.

The Triton has small buttons. I have big fingers. Surprisingly, this does not seem to be an issue, as I have not yet had the misfortune of mis-keying anything.

Several reviewers have complained that the menu system on the Triton is confusing, unintuitive and hard to use. I did not find this to be the case. I can simply say they are different than Garmin's implementations. That is neither good nor bad - just, different. Once used to them, this unit is no less intuitive than any other unit.

Navigation is straightforward and easy. When navigating I have found the unit to be on par with my Garmin GPSMap 60CSx, which is usually fairly accurate. I've no complaints in this regard.

My disappointment with the Triton mostly involve what's [not] in the box and the software that the computer uses to interact with it. There is a single CD in the box that includes PDF versions of the manual. There are no printed manuals in the box, at all. This is ok, but other units include a manual so it would be nice if this one did too. There is also a link to the website where you can download Vantage Point, the software for working with the unit. The software is 42MB, and I am on dial-up. Even including an older version would have been nice since there is plenty of room on the CD for it...

When the software is loaded on a Windows Vista machine, system behavior becomes very sluggish, mouse movement being choppy and COM port communications getting interruptions - enough interruptions to disconnect from the Internet. Though the software has eye appeal and offers a lot of functionality for dealing with the GPS, it drips of slowness. When sending caches to the unit, it sends at a rate of about 1 every 5-10 seconds, which means sending 500 at a time would take a good deal of time. That said, geocache information stops a little shy of being a paperless solution - the unit retains description, terrain/difficulty, owner and hint information, but it does not offer previous logs, sizes or other important bits of information. It's a good reference in the field but not sufficient to go true paperless.

Though there is a place on the bottom of the unit for a lanyard, it is disappointing that there is none in the box.

One area of real concern for me is the connection interface for the unit. The connector on the unit is exposed and uncovered, with nothing to keep it from getting dirty. If nothing else there should be a rubber flap over it, or a cover, or *something*.

This is actually a nice unit, with a decent feature set and good accuracy. Magellan cut some corners and left out some details that keep this from being a great unit. The technology is there. The design is there. The details are not. Hopefully Magellan will close the gap on these details soon.
text_fidelity_b: Magellan Triton 400 Waterproof Hiking GPS

text_fidelity_a: Fire TV Stick streaming device with Alexa built in, includes Alexa Voice Remote, HD, latest release I've been using Amazon FireStick and Amazon Prime video exclusively for TV viewing for almost 9 years. I don't even have cable, and I don't miss it a bit. In all that time, I only replaced my FireStick once, and that was because I stupidly lost the remote, and it arrived in about 4 hours thanks to Amazon Prime Now. It is high quality and very easy to use. But like most tech companies, Amazon keeps producing "upgrades" to the Prime Video channel software that sacrifice basic functions for bells and whistles. Movies are no longer included on the RECENTS list, and since I view documentaries I use to teach in my college classrooms, I do sometimes need to view a film more than once to ensure my notes are correct. Also, if I fell asleep watching a movie, it used to be easy to find it to watch again. Sometimes, even a TV series I'm watching disappears from the RECENTS list, even though it was there the day before. As with most "upgrades," each version gets a little bit worse in terms of basic functionality. I never upgrade software when I have a choice, but we're not given a choice in this case. Tech companies need to learn the expression "if it ain't broke, don't 'fix' it."
text_fidelity_b: Fire TV Stick streaming device with Alexa built in, includes Alexa Voice Remote, HD, latest release
